1.5 — Movement II: Speed, deltaTime & Tuning

Your character moves — but it walks through walls, and it does not yet feel like anything. Today you fix a speed bug you can probably already feel, learn what Time.deltaTime is really doing for you, and tune the character until it feels right to control.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“why does my character move faster diagonally, and how do I fix it?”Full walkthrough
Break It Down~10 minFull walkthrough

My character moves faster on the diagonal than it does in a straight line — "why does my character move faster diagonally, and how do I fix it?" The movement from 1.4 already works, and that is exactly what makes the wrongness hard to see.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Read which way the player is pushingThe two Input.GetAxis reads from 1.4, assigned to the inputX and inputY fields you already declared in the class body. Unchanged, and nothing here is the bug.Read: the Input.GetAxis("Horizontal") row in the quick reference.
  2. Build a direction vector out of the two numbersPack both axes into one Vector2. At this point it is pure direction — no speed and no time multiplied in — and its length is whatever the input happens to be, which is the whole problem.Read: the Vector2 row in the quick reference, and the vector you built yourself in 1.4.
  3. Rescale that vector to a length of exactly 1direction = direction.normalized; keeps the arrow pointing the same way and throws its length away, so "up and right" is (0.707, 0.707) instead of (1, 1). This is the fix, and it is general, not a special case for diagonals: eight directions, a half-pushed stick, anything.Read: the (a - b).normalized row in the quick reference — direction, length exactly 1, whatever you hand it.
  4. Scale that unit direction into a distance, and apply itOne multiplication: direction * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime. Because the direction is always length 1, this distance is identical whichever way you are facing. Then transform.Translate applies it, exactly as it did in 1.4.Read: the Time.deltaTime and transform.Translate(v) rows in the quick reference.

Four parts, and the new one sits in the middle rather than at the end. The vector from 1.4 was two numbers stapled together, which is fine until you do arithmetic with them: (1, 0) is length 1 and (0, 1) is length 1, but (1, 1) is 1.41 — so pressing two keys moved you 41% further. A direction and a distance are different quantities, and the moment you keep them in separate parts, the fix is one line.

The test: is "which way" still in the same part as "how far"? If you cannot point at the one line where speed is applied, the direction and the distance are still tangled — and that tangling is what made the bug invisible in 1.4.

Read the Docs ~15 min

In Unity there is rarely just one way to solve a problem. Each of these four movement techniques exists because it solves a problem the others handle badly. Read the trade-offs — including which ones demand a component your character does not have yet:

TechniqueHow it worksNeeds a Rigidbody2D?Best for
transform.Translate(vector) Directly offsets the object's coordinates. Skips the physics engine entirely. No Simple top-down games, moving UI, linear projectiles, bullets without gravity
Rigidbody2D.MovePosition(position) Drives the physics body to a target position along the path. A Dynamic body is stopped cleanly by solid colliders on the way; a Kinematic body ignores them and arrives anyway. Yes — and Dynamic if you want a wall to stop it Moving platforms, lifts and scripted set pieces that must arrive at an exact position rather than travel at a speed
Rigidbody2D.linearVelocity = vector Assigns a velocity to the physics body. The physics engine does the moving — and unlike Translate, the number is per second, not per frame. Yes — and Dynamic if you want a wall to stop it Snappy platformers, arcade physics, carrying momentum across surfaces
Rigidbody2D.AddForce(vector) Applies a physical push or impulse, factoring in mass, drag, and inertia. Yes — and Dynamic; a Kinematic body ignores forces entirely Jumping, thrusters, ice physics, knockback from explosions or enemy hits

Note what MovePosition buys you: it drives the body along the path rather than teleporting it there, so whatever is in the way gets a say. On a Dynamic body that is the difference between walking into a wall and walking through one — but the call is not what stops you. Put the same line on a Kinematic body and it walks through the wall exactly as Translate did.

Do not switch methods today. You have not added the component three of these four need, and you have a good reason not to yet — you will add it in 2.1 for a different purpose entirely (picking up coins), and 2.2 is where you will use it to stop walking through walls. Today you are learning what the options are, so that decision is an informed one when it arrives.

Socratic: Choosing the Right Tool for the Job

  1. You proved in 1.4 that transform.Translate walks through walls. MovePosition does get stopped by a wall — but only when the body is Dynamic. In your own words, what is that call consulting that Translate never consults?
  2. Look at the third column. Three of these four options need a component your Player does not have yet. What would you have to add to your character, and where would you add it — on the Player, or on the child Sprite?
  3. Why would a game about a spaceship drifting through space prefer AddForce over Translate?
Build It With MeFull walkthrough

The question this answers“why does my character move faster diagonally, and how do I fix it?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. You already have working movement from 1.4. This walkthrough replaces two of those lines with a clearer version that moves at exactly the same speed in every direction.

Step 1See the problem first

Hold W and D together. You are moving up and right at the same time — but how far are you actually travelling?

// Straight right:      (1, 0)   -> length 1
// Straight up:         (0, 1)   -> length 1
// Up and right:        (1, 1)   -> length 1.41
  1. 1Pressing D alone gives a direction of length 1.
  2. 2Pressing W alone gives a direction of length 1.
  3. 3Pressing both gives a direction of length 1.41, not 1. Your character is travelling 41% further per frame in that direction — so diagonal movement is 41% faster than it should be.

Step 2Separate direction from speed

In 1.4 you multiplied the input by speed in two separate places. Pull those apart: first work out which way to go, then decide how far.

        Vector2 direction = new Vector2(inputX, inputY);

        direction = direction.normalized;

        Vector2 movement = direction * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime;

        transform.Translate(movement);
  1. 1Builds a vector pointing whichever way the player is holding. At this point it is pure direction — no speed, no time. Its length is whatever the input happens to be.
  2. 3The fix. .normalized keeps the vector pointing the same way but rescales it to a length of exactly 1. Now "up and right" is (0.707, 0.707) instead of (1, 1) — same direction, correct length.This is the general solution, not a special case for diagonals. It works for eight directions, for a controller stick pushed halfway, for anything. Notice there is no second Vector2 in front of direction — the variable already exists, so this line assigns to it, exactly like inputX from 1.3.
  3. 5Now scale that unit direction up to a real distance: one second's worth of travel (moveSpeed), scaled down to a single frame (Time.deltaTime).One clean multiplication replaces the two long lines from 1.4. Because direction is always length 1, this distance is identical no matter which way you are facing.
  4. 7Applies it, exactly as before. This line has not changed at all.
Check your work: the finished filebuild it as you read — then open this to check every line

Compare against your own file. The only lines that should differ from 1.4 are the three that now build direction and movement — your fields, your input reads, and your transform.Translate are unchanged.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeed = 5f;

    private float inputX;
    private float inputY;

    void Update()
    {
        inputX = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
        inputY = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");

        Vector2 direction = new Vector2(inputX, inputY);
        direction = direction.normalized;

        Vector2 movement = direction * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime;

        transform.Translate(movement);
    }
}
What deltaTime is really doing ~10 min

You have been typing * Time.deltaTime since 1.4 because you were told to. Here is the actual reason, in one paragraph you should be able to repeat back.

Update() does not run at a fixed rate. On your laptop it might run 60 times a second; on the machine next to you, 240; on a phone that is getting hot, 30. If your code moved the character moveSpeed units every time Update runs, then the character would travel four times as far per second on the 240 FPS machine. The game would literally be easier or harder depending on the computer.

Time.deltaTime is the number of seconds the last frame took. At 60 FPS it is about 0.0167; at 240 FPS it is about 0.0042. Multiplying by it converts "this much per frame" into "this much per second" — which is the same number on every machine. deltaTime is an abstraction: it hides the messy, unpredictable reality of frame timing behind a single number you can just multiply by.

Tuning Lab: Find the Feel ~20 min

Numbers you guess at in the editor are almost never the numbers that feel right in motion. Professional designers tune while the game runs. Here is the workflow you will use for the rest of the year:

  1. Press Play in Unity, then walk around the overworld.
  2. While the game is still running, select the Player in the Hierarchy and change moveSpeed in the Inspector. Walk again. Too sluggish?
  3. Try a much larger number. Notice how twitchy and uncontrollable it becomes.
  4. Bisect your way to a number that feels right for exploring a world this size. Try somewhere between 4 and 7 as a starting point.
  5. Write the number down, exit Play mode, and set that value in edit mode so it persists.
Remember the play-mode rule from 1.2: any value you change while the Play button is blue resets when you stop the game. Use play mode to find your number, then enter it in edit mode to keep it.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Compare four ways to move an object in Unity: Translate, MovePosition, linearVelocity, AddForce
  • Say which of the four need a Rigidbody2D, which body type a wall can actually stop, and explain what moving along a path does differently from a teleport
  • Explain, in your own words, why (1, 1) is a longer vector than (1, 0) — and what .normalized does about it
  • Explain how Time.deltaTime produces the same real-world speed at different frame rates
  • Explain the relationship between a code default and a serialized Inspector value
  • Save your tuned speed and commit your changes
